description: The EU's system of autonomous restrictive measures adopted under CFSP, applying asset freezes, travel bans, and sector-specific prohibitions against designated persons, entities, and states.

canonical_name: EU Regulation 269/2014 — Russia Crimea Asset Freeze
description: Council Regulation (EU) No 269/2014 of 17 March 2014 imposing restrictive measures in respect of actions undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine. Provides for asset freezes and travel bans on designated individuals.

Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 of 31 July 2014 concerning restrictive measures in view of Russia's actions destabilising Ukraine. Imposes sectoral prohibitions on finance, energy, defence, and technology sectors. Significantly expanded since 2022.

Council Regulation (EC) No 765/2006 of 18 May 2006 concerning restrictive measures against President Lukashenko and certain officials of Belarus. Significantly expanded following the 2020 election and 2021 Ryanair incident.
Council Regulation (EU) No 359/2011 of 12 April 2011 concerning restrictive measures directed against certain persons, entities and bodies in view of the situation in Iran.

Council Regulation (EC) 2271/96 of 22 November 1996 protecting against the effects of the extra-territorial application of legislation adopted by a third country and actions based thereon or resulting therefrom. Primarily targets OFAC/US secondary sanctions extraterritorial effect.

UN Security Council framework of targeted financial sanctions adopted under Chapter VII of the UN Charter. Implemented by EU regulations and national law. Core regimes: Al-Qaeda/ISIS (UNSCR 1267/2253), DPRK (UNSCR 1718), Iran (UNSCR 1737/2231).

UN Security Council Resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011), 2253 (2015) establishing the Al-Qaeda/ISIS consolidated sanctions list. Requires member states to freeze assets, ban travel, and impose arms embargoes on listed individuals and entities.

UN Security Council Resolution 1718 (2006) establishing the DPRK sanctions regime in response to nuclear weapons testing. Mandates asset freezes, travel bans, and arms embargoes on designated North Korean individuals and entities.
UN Security Council Resolution 1737 (2006) establishing the Iran nuclear-related sanctions regime. Targets individuals and entities associated with Iran's nuclear and ballistic missile programmes.

The US Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) administers and enforces economic and trade sanctions based on US foreign policy and national security goals. Issues Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list, sectoral sanctions, and secondary sanctions.

An individual or entity formally listed by a sanctions authority (EU Council, UN Security Council, OFAC, OFSI) as subject to restrictive measures including asset freeze, travel ban, or sector-specific prohibitions.

Prohibition on making funds and economic resources available to a designated person or entity, and requirement to freeze all funds and economic resources owned or controlled by designated persons. Core obligation under EU, UN, and US sanctions regimes.
The prohibition on directly or indirectly making funds or economic resources available to, or for the benefit of, designated persons and entities. Broader than the freeze obligation itself.
Prohibition on entry to or transit through Member State territories for designated individuals. Applies to persons listed under EU autonomous sanctions and UN sanctions as transposed.

Prohibition on the sale, supply, transfer, or export of arms, military equipment, and related materiel to designated countries or entities. A standard component of UN and EU country sanctions regimes.

Sanctions specifically targeting identified individuals and entities (as opposed to comprehensive embargoes). TFS includes asset freezes and funds availability prohibitions. Required by FATF Recommendations 6 and 7.

The EU's official list of all persons, groups, and entities subject to EU financial sanctions, maintained and published by the European Commission Financial Sanctions database (EUSANCTIONS). Consolidates all country-specific and thematic regimes.

Authorised exception to a sanctions prohibition, granted by competent national authorities. Types include: humanitarian derogations, diplomatic mission exceptions, judicial process access, and pre-existing contractual obligations.

A time-limited licence authorising continuation of otherwise prohibited transactions for the purpose of terminating contracts or relationships with newly designated persons. Typically 30–90 days. Available under OFAC and many EU regimes.

canonical_name: OFAC SDN List — Specially Designated Nationals
description: OFAC's primary sanctions list identifying individuals and companies whose assets are blocked and with whom US persons are generally prohibited from dealing. Approximately 12,000+ entries. Consolidated SDN list updated frequently.

canonical_name: CAPTA List — Correspondent Account or Payable-Through Account Sanctions
description: OFAC list targeting foreign financial institutions prohibited from maintaining correspondent or payable-through accounts at US financial institutions. A more targeted tool than full SDN designation.

Sanctions targeting specific economic sectors rather than designated individuals. EU Russia Regulation 833/2014 and OFAC's Sectoral Sanctions Identifications (SSI) list are primary examples. Restrict debt, equity financing, and services in targeted sectors.
EU framework under which restrictive measures (sanctions) are adopted by the EU Council. CFSP decisions are implemented as directly applicable EU regulations under Art. 215 TFEU.

The EU's largest sanctions regime, significantly expanded from 2022 onwards in response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Includes individual designations (Reg. 269/2014) and sectoral prohibitions (Reg. 833/2014) covering finance, energy, transport, technology, and luxury goods.

UN and EU sanctions targeting North Korea's weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile programmes. Among the world's most comprehensive sectoral sanctions. EU implemented via Council Regulation (EU) 2017/1509.

EU and UN sanctions targeting Iran's nuclear programme and human rights violations. EU nuclear-related sanctions partially suspended under JCPOA (2015), re-imposed from 2019. Human rights sanctions maintained separately under Reg. 359/2011.
EU restrictive measures adopted in response to the February 2021 military coup in Myanmar/Burma. Includes individual designations of military leaders and sectoral prohibitions on military equipment.

EU restrictive measures against the Syrian regime established from 2011 following violent repression of civilian protests. Council Regulation (EU) No 36/2012. Includes oil sector embargo and individual asset freezes.
EU restrictive measures against Belarus established from 2006, significantly expanded since 2020 elections and 2021 forced landing of Ryanair flight. Council Regulation (EC) No 765/2006.
EU targeted financial sanctions and travel bans against individuals responsible for human rights violations and undermining democracy in Venezuela. Council Regulation (EU) 2017/2063.

Prohibition under Regulation 833/2014 on import of crude oil and petroleum products from Russia, investment in Russian oil sector, and provision of related services. One of the most significant EU economic sanctions measures.

Prohibition under Regulation 833/2014 on transactions with designated Russian financial institutions, purchase of transferable securities, and money market instruments. Applies to listed Russian state-owned banks.

All EU sanctions regulations contain an explicit prohibition on participating, knowingly and intentionally, in activities the object or effect of which is to circumvent sanctions measures. Circumvention includes use of third-country intermediaries, shell companies, and nominee arrangements.

Property and interests of designated persons are blocked if the designated person owns, directly or indirectly, 50% or more of that property. EU applies the same principle. Requires look-through analysis of ownership chains.

EU sanctions prohibitions apply to: (1) EU nationals anywhere in the world; (2) persons on EU territory; (3) EU-incorporated legal entities; (4) transactions in EUR (settled via EU correspondent banks). Extraterritorial effect is therefore significant.

Financial institutions and other obliged parties must report information useful for ensuring compliance with sanctions to national competent authorities and provide frozen assets information. Also required when encountering a potential match.

EU sanctions are enforced at national level by designated competent authorities (FI, Finanstilsynet, etc.) and criminal prosecution authorities. Criminal penalties for violations vary across Member States. EU working to harmonise sanctions penalties.

metadata.pending: EU Directive on criminal penalties for sanctions violations

description: Controls on export of goods and technology that can be used for both civilian and military purposes. Closely related to sanctions on DPRK and Iran. Governed by EU Dual-Use Regulation (EU) 2021/821 and national export control laws.

Mandatory process for financial institutions and other obliged parties to check customers, counterparties, transactions, and beneficial owners against consolidated sanctions lists (EU, OFAC SDN, UN, national). Must be conducted at onboarding and on an ongoing basis.

Operational process for freezing funds and economic resources of newly designated persons: immediate account suspension, notification to competent authority, cessation of all transactions, and reporting of frozen amounts.

Process for applying for a licence/derogation to carry out an otherwise prohibited sanctions transaction. Submitted to national competent authority (e.g., Finansinspektionen in Sweden, OFSI in UK). Humanitarian, diplomatic, and legal access grounds.

When a sanctions match or sanctions circumvention suspicion is identified, the obliged entity must both freeze assets AND file a suspicious activity report with the FIU. Dual obligation: sanctions compliance + AML reporting.

Formal application to competent authority for authorisation to perform otherwise prohibited transactions. Under OFAC: General Licences (pre-authorised) and Specific Licences (case-by-case). Under EU: submitted to national competent authority.

OFAC-issued authorisation that allows a category of transactions otherwise prohibited without need for an individual licence. Published in the Code of Federal Regulations or as standalone documents. Examples: food, medicine, journalistic activities.

Individual OFAC authorisation for a specific transaction or category of transactions. Must be applied for using OFAC's licence application system. OFAC targets 90-day review for complete applications.

Algorithmic process for comparing customer/counterparty names against sanctions lists, accounting for spelling variations, transliterations, aliases, and date-of-birth matching. Typically uses threshold-based fuzzy matching (e.g., 80% similarity).

Operational process for reviewing, documenting, and clearing sanctions screening alerts that do not relate to an actual designated person. Must be documented with rationale. Persistent false positives may indicate tuning issues.

Process for re-screening existing customer base against updated sanctions lists following new designations. EU sanctions lists update frequently (often with 24-hour implementation deadline). OFAC SDN updates multiple times per week.

AMLR Article 6 requires obliged entities to comply with targeted financial sanctions without delay when designated persons are involved. Links AML framework to sanctions compliance. Screening and SAR obligations interact.

FATF Recommendation 6 requires countries to implement targeted financial sanctions to comply with UN Security Council Resolutions on terrorism financing (UNSCR 1267/2253 and 1373). Must implement without delay — same-day implementation expected.

FATF Recommendation 7 requires countries to implement targeted financial sanctions to comply with UN Security Council Resolutions on proliferation financing (DPRK and Iran WMD). Requires without-delay implementation.

Intersection of EU AML regulation (AMLR 2024/1624) and EU sanctions: AMLR Art. 6 requires TFS compliance; sanctions-related suspicion must be reported as SAR; sanctions screening is a component of CDD; PEP screening overlaps with sanctions screening.

CASPs licensed under MiCA Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 are obliged entities under AMLR and must screen crypto-asset transfers against sanctions lists. Travel Rule (TFR Regulation) requires originator/beneficiary sanctions checks.

Critical ICT third-party providers (CTPPs) designated under DORA may be subject to sanctions. Financial entities must ensure their CTPP contracts allow termination if the provider is sanctioned. Sanctions screening applies to ICT vendor relationships.

The EU's diplomatic service, which drafts EU sanctions proposals in coordination with the EU Council. The EEAS Foreign Policy Instruments service manages the sanctions database and technical implementation.

canonical_name: Council of the European Union (Sanctions Adopting Body)
description: The EU Council formally adopts EU sanctions (CFSP Decisions and implementing Regulations) by unanimity for CFSP decisions, and qualified majority for implementing regulations. Responsible for listing and delisting decisions.

canonical_name: OFSI — UK Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation
description: UK Treasury body responsible for implementing and enforcing financial sanctions in the United Kingdom. Issues licences for otherwise prohibited transactions. Maintains UK sanctions list (post-Brexit, separate from EU list).

canonical_name: OFAC — US Office of Foreign Assets Control
description: US Treasury body administering and enforcing economic and trade sanctions. Maintains the SDN list, issues General and Specific Licences, and enforces with civil and criminal penalties. Significant extraterritorial reach via USD clearing.

Subsidiary bodies of the UN Security Council responsible for designating individuals and entities on UN sanctions lists, monitoring implementation, and processing humanitarian exemption requests. Each regime has its own committee.

Swedish financial supervisory authority responsible for supervising compliance with EU sanctions by Swedish financial institutions. Coordinates with Swedish police (Polismyndigheten) and Riksbanken. Reports to government.

Finnish Financial Supervisory Authority responsible for supervising compliance with EU sanctions by Finnish financial institutions. Works with Finnish Ministry for Foreign Affairs on national implementation.

Norwegian Financial Supervisory Authority responsible for supervising sanctions compliance by Norwegian financial institutions. Norway implements UN sanctions and mirrors most EU sanctions as an EEA member.

Danish Financial Supervisory Authority responsible for supervising EU sanctions compliance by Danish financial institutions. Works under the Sanctions Act (Sanktionsloven) for national implementation.
